1	# Growth — dedup local packs against the canon (per repo)
2	
3	The growth lifecycle's pruning stage: reconcile this repo's **local packs** against the shared **canon** it
4	consumes (Claudinite, vendored read-only), pruning local items — a pack's prose line, or a whole local check —
5	the canon now covers. It opens a PR against the repo's default branch for the owner to approve. Often there's
6	nothing to prune, and that's fine. You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue, whose
7	**Context** is **binding scope — not a hint** (the executor will not let you re-decide or widen it).
8	
9	> This task only prunes local packs against the canon; lifting local items up into the canon is the central
10	> promote task's job (canon-side).
11	
12	## Conventions used in this doc
13	
14	- **Default branch.** `main` stands for **this repository's default branch** — substitute whatever the repo uses.
15	- **GitHub access is MCP-native.** Updating the tracking issue and opening the PR go through the session's
16	  **GitHub MCP tools** (`mcp__github__*`). The unattended run has no shell GitHub access — the shell reaches
17	  only a git-over-HTTPS proxy scoped to one repo, with no REST credential — so never reach for `gh`/`curl` or
18	  a cross-repo clone.
19	- **The mounted canon.** The exact canon revision this repo currently consumes — compare against *that*, not a
20	  live fetch. It is what `.claudinite/shared/` holds at the mount's stamp (a promotion is visible here only
21	  once baselining has converged the mount to include it). Prune only against what the repo actually mounts.
22	- **The dispatch's Context narrows the *yardstick*, never the local surface.** When the Context names
23	  newly-changed canon packs ("Re-check local items against these newly-changed canon packs: …"), **those packs
24	  are this run's entire yardstick**: every prune must cite a line or rule id from one of *them*, and you never
25	  widen the comparison to the rest of the mounted canon. What is *not* narrowed is the local side — **every**
26	  local item is in play against those packs, whatever it is about. (Local pack names are unrelated to canon
27	  pack names, so there is nothing to match up.) A dispatch with **no** Context block carries no such bound: the
28	  precondition emits the list only when the mounted canon moved, and its other arm — the repo's own local packs
29	  changed — deliberately emits none, so that run compares the fresh local items against the whole mounted canon.
30	- **The repo's local packs.** The set identified in [this pack's README](../../README.md#identifying-a-projects-capture-surface-its-local-packs) —
31	  everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the
32	  rename window). That's the corpus this task prunes within; the read-only mounted canon elsewhere under
33	  `.claudinite/` is never a prune target, only the yardstick you prune *against*.
34	
35	## What it does: prune / rephrase local packs the canon now covers
36	
37	When the canon has **absorbed** a practice a local doc still carries — most often an item the central promote
38	task lifted up and the canon now owns — the local copy is redundant. This task:
39	
40	- **Removes** the now-duplicated local item, since the canon is the single source of truth for portable rules.
41	- **Strips** a *partially* covered item down to its residue — when an item's general half is now canon-owned
42	  but it still carries a stronger point about a narrower case, **delete the portable half in place and keep
43	  only the residue**. A strip is a **deletion that shrinks the entry**: lead with the residual point (using the
44	  file's own `(canon)` tag convention if it has one), never with a meta-line like "this rule is portable
45	  (canon)", and **never re-state the now-canon rule, its fix, or which pack owns it** — carrying it is exactly
46	  what you are removing. If your "strip" adds words or restates the canon, you have *un*-deduped the item: keep
47	  the pre-edit text instead.
48	- **Rephrases** a local procedure *only* when the canon's wording of the same idea has changed, so the local
49	  packs stay consistent with the canon they point at — a rephrase tracks a wording drift; it never grows the
50	  entry and never re-imports canon prose.
51	
52	**Keep a local item only if it says *more* than the canon — not merely says it more specifically.** Every
53	local item is more specific than the canon, so specificity alone is never the test. Distinguish two cases:
54	
55	- **The general rule in local dress** — it makes the canon's point but leans on this repo's classes, files, or
56	  names to make it. Once the canon covers the point, those names were only illustration: prune it.
57	- **A stronger point about a narrower case** — it asserts something the canon's general rule leaves out: a
58	  tighter constraint, a sharper claim that holds for this repo's narrower situation. Keep it.
59	
60	So ask not "is it specific" (it always is) but "does it only lean on specific names to make the general point,
61	or does it make a point the canon doesn't?" Prune the first; keep the second.
62	
63	## A canon check covers an item too — and more strongly than prose
64	
65	The canon carries rules as **conformance checks**, not only prose. A local item is covered when a canon check
66	*enforces* it — stronger coverage than a stated line, since the rule runs on every session and CI pass.
67	Consult the machine-readable rule catalog (`node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs --list`:
68	id, severity, description, doc pointer — it lists the active local packs' own checks too) alongside the prose
69	corpus, and when a check covers the item, **quote the rule id** where you'd otherwise quote a canon line. This
70	cuts both ways: a **local pack's own check** is redundant once a canon check enforces the same rule — prune the
71	local `.mjs` (and drop it from `pack.mjs` + its fixture) exactly as you'd prune a duplicated prose line. The
72	keep-test above is unchanged: a local item that says *more* than the check detects (a stronger point about a
73	narrower case) stays.
74	
75	## Discipline
76	
77	- **Only remove a local item you can show the mounted canon genuinely covers — quote the canon line (or the
78	  covering check's rule id).** When unsure, leave it; a wrongful prune deletes a real local lesson.
79	- **Open a single PR against `main`** from a per-run-unique branch (see
80	  [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)) — one PR for the
81	  whole run's prunes, not one per item — never a direct push. This is an unattended task, on a capable model, and a **wrongful prune
82	  deletes a real local lesson**, so — unlike [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md), whose additive edits
83	  ride a PR that auto-merges after CI — this task keeps a **human** approval gate (its declared outcome ceiling
84	  is `open-pr`: it may open a PR but never merge it). **Put the issue reference in the commit message** —
85	  `Refs #<n>` for this task's tracking issue (below), in the commit itself, not only the PR body. The repo's
86	  `basics` `task-lifecycle` check gates a PR on its commits referencing an issue, so a prune commit that cites
87	  none reds the repo's CI and blocks the merge.
88	- If an edit touches something a test reads, run the repo's offline test suite and keep it green before pushing.
89	
90	## Tracking
91	
92	The task's standing log is the issue titled exactly, in this repo:
93	
94	> **Claudinite tracker: Growth Dedup**
95	
96	Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number**. A run that finds no issue under
97	the exact title just creates one (closed). **Never open, close, or reopen it** afterward — its state carries no
98	meaning, only the log does. Log each run that changed a doc as a **dated comment** — naming what was pruned and
99	the canon line that now covers it. A run that prunes nothing logs nothing.
100	
101	## Run on a capable model
102	
103	Proving the mounted canon genuinely covers a local item before pruning it — and telling "the canon now owns
104	this" from "the canon states this too generally, keep the local cut" — is a **judgment call**. A downgraded
105	model prunes a real lesson; the review PR is a backstop, but a wrongful prune is easy to wave through in
106	review, so don't lean on it. This task declares `agent_model: opus`; the executor dispatches its subagent there.
107	
108	## What this task must never do
109	
110	- **Never edit the read-only canon** — it only prunes the repo's *local packs* against it.
111	- **Never merge its own PR** — the human approval gate is the whole point (`outcome: open-pr`).
112	- **Never prune a local item without quoting the mounted-canon line (or covering check rule id) that covers
113	  it** — when unsure, leave it.
114	- **Never widen the dispatch's Context.** If it named the changed canon packs, a prune citing coverage from
115	  any *other* canon pack is out of scope for this run — leave the item; the cycle that moves that pack will
116	  reach it.
117	- **Never prune a local item that makes a stronger point about a narrower case** than the canon — that isn't
118	  redundancy. (A local item that only restates the canon in repo-specific names *is* prunable once the canon
119	  covers the point.)
120	- **Never let a dedup edit grow an entry or re-import canon prose.** Every action this task takes *removes*
121	  portable text: a Remove deletes the item, a Strip deletes its portable half, a Rephrase tracks a wording
122	  drift without adding. An edit that leaves an entry the same size or larger, re-quotes the now-canon rule, or
123	  names the owning pack's fix is a **corruption, not a dedup** — the exact inverse of the job. When in doubt
124	  about a kept item, leave it byte-for-byte unchanged rather than "reconcile" its wording. The
125	  `dedup-prune-integrity` check (`basics`-style work-scope rule, this pack) is the backstop: it reds the
126	  session when a dedup-labeled commit grows a local-pack prose file, or when any change adds a line that
127	  restates a canon rule ("… is portable (canon)", "… pack owns …").

A source never re-reads what the page 218 already says about itself, and the generic extractor may never know about a 219 specific site. 220 - **Being supported is DECLARED, never derived from the extractors.** 221 `supportedDomains` in `extension/host-lists.json` is the one list of hosts 222 we claim, read directly by the toolbar worker and the popup. Never add a second 223 list, and never register a placeholder source just to make a host count as 224 supported. The check's failure message is where the rule lives now and its header 251 comment is where the rationale lives, so a paragraph restating either pays twice 252 and is the drift trap waiting to spring. Before concluding prose is the only 253 carrier, look at the pack's **skills** too — an activity-scoped skill often 254 already holds the map a rule is repeating. Whether a check covers a rule is a 260 judgment about meaning, so this test is applied by a reader, not mechanized. 261 262 **Three kinds never land here, however strong the evidence** — filter on what a 263 lesson is *about* before picking a mechanism: 264 265 - **The owner's personal preferences** (which word means "merge it", tone, 266 summary style). 14	The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.
15	
16	Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.
17	
18	When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.
19	
20	When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."
21	
22	Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.
23	
24	Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.
25	
26	Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.
27	
28	When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.
29	
30	An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.
31	
32	# The task lifecycle
33	
34	The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.
35	
36	For every new task:
37	
38	1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
39	2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
40	3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.
41	########## chrome-extension/RULES.md
42	# Chrome extensions
43	
44	Portable, project-agnostic practices for building Chrome (and Chromium) extensions — manifest versions, background/service workers, content scripts, permissions, packaging and store review — true for any extension read cold.
45	
46	> **Releasing, versioning, and Chrome Web Store publication are standardized** — before building or changing any release/publish machinery in an extension repo, read the [chrome-extension-release standard](../chrome-extension-release/RELEASE.md) (its pack, declared when you're ready to ship) and copy its canonical workflows instead of re-deriving them.
47	
48	- An MV3 service worker's relative paths resolve against the worker's **own** file location, not the extension root. Any path handed to a Chrome API (`importScripts`, `action.setIcon`) or `fetch` must be extension-root absolute — a leading slash, or `chrome.runtime.getURL(...)`. A bare relative path fails silently: it can abort the worker on import, or make an API call reject while the worker keeps running.
49	- `chrome.events.UrlFilter`'s host operators are **raw string matches, not domain-boundary matches** — `hostSuffix: "example.com"` also matches `evilexample.com`, and `declarativeContent`'s `PageStateMatcher.pageUrl` gates an action icon or page condition on exactly these filters. To mean *apex-or-any-subdomain*, combine `hostEquals: "example.com"` with `hostSuffix: ".example.com"` (the leading dot forces a label boundary); never gate a security- or origin-sensitive behavior on a bare `hostSuffix`.
50	- A shared global assembled by multiple injected content-script files, re-injected into the page on every activation (e.g. every popup open), must be **augmented**, never replaced — merge onto it (e.g. `Object.assign`), not `globalThis.X = {...}`, or each newly-injected file wipes what earlier files already attached. Likewise reset any state a file accumulates on each injection (e.g. a list a source pushes into) at load time.
51	- Introspecting an MV3 service worker over CDP (`Runtime.evaluate` inside it) has two traps: `chrome.*` callback APIs don't reliably settle when awaited with `awaitPromise: true` (a hang with no internal timeout) — build the awaited signal from plain promises (`fetch`/`OffscreenCanvas`) instead of a `chrome.*` callback; and a bare top-level `function`/`const` isn't reachable from an injected evaluate — expose what the probe reads as an explicit `globalThis.x = …`. A dormant worker also has no globals until it re-runs its top level, and attaching to it is what starts that — so poll for the global rather than reading it once immediately after attaching.
52	- To authenticate an extension to a **JWT-validating** backend (an API Gateway JWT authorizer, any OIDC-validating server), obtain a Google **ID token** with `chrome.identity.launchWebAuthFlow` (`response_type=id_token`) against a Google Cloud OAuth client of type **Web application**, redirect to `https://<extension-id>.chromiumapp.org/` (from `chrome.identity.getRedirectURL()`), scope `openid email profile`, and **verify the returned `nonce`**. Do **not** use `chrome.identity.getAuthToken` — it returns an opaque OAuth *access* token (no verifiable signature/`iss`/`aud`) that a JWT authorizer rejects. Pin the extension id with a manifest `key` so the redirect URI stays fixed.
53	- MV3 loads ES modules natively — don't add a bundler just to use `import`/`export`. Declare the service worker `"type": "module"` and load page/side-panel scripts with `<script type="module">`; relative imports resolve within the packaged extension.
54	- A silent token refresh (`launchWebAuthFlow({interactive:false})`) must request `prompt=none`; `prompt=consent` always needs interaction and therefore always fails silently — reserve it (or omit `prompt`) for the interactive fallback.
55	- On a **silent** token refresh with more than one account signed in, pass the remembered account's email as `login_hint` — otherwise the provider can't tell which session to reuse and forces an interactive account-picker. Persist the non-secret email from the first successful sign-in.
56	- Extension storage is unencrypted, so treat tokens as secrets at rest: keep the bearer/ID token in in-memory `chrome.storage.session` (cleared on browser exit) and persist only non-secret identifiers (e.g. the account email) to `chrome.storage.local`. Don't switch to a refresh-token flow just to survive restarts — that puts a longer-lived credential on disk; re-run the silent flow instead.
57	- To run a content script on arbitrary third-party pages **without** an install-time host warning, request access at runtime: declare the origins under `optional_host_permissions` plus the (silent) `scripting` permission, call `chrome.permissions.request()` **synchronously inside a real foreground user gesture** (Chrome rejects the request from a service-worker message handler), then register the script dynamically with `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts()` — never a static `content_scripts` entry. The grant can be revoked from `chrome://extensions` out from under you, so on every service-worker start reconcile your stored enabled-flag against the permission actually granted and re-register (or clean up) to match.
58	- MV3 gives the side panel no is-open/close API, and an action popup suppresses `action.onClicked` — so to know whether your panel is open, have the panel open a `Port` on load and read its connect/disconnect as open/closed. Opening the panel programmatically needs `chrome.sidePanel.open()` (Chrome 116+), so raise `minimum_chrome_version` accordingly.
59	- `host_permissions` does not bypass CORS. Listing a host lets the extension's fetches *reach* it, but the server must still return CORS headers for the extension origin (`chrome-extension://<id>`) or the request fails in-browser. Conversely, don't add a `host_permissions` entry merely to reach *your own* backend: if it already returns permissive CORS the fetch succeeds without it, and the entry only adds a scary install-time host-access warning.
60	- A **registered or static content script runs as a *classic* script — it can't be an ES module.** `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts` and static `content_scripts` inject their files as classic scripts (there is no `type: 'module'` mode, unlike a page's `<script type="module">` or the module service worker), so a top-level `import` in one throws `Uncaught SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module` — **in the host page's console, not the extension's**. To load module code without a bundler, register a tiny **classic loader** whose only statement is a *dynamic* `import(chrome.runtime.getURL('…'))`: dynamic `import()` is legal in a classic script, and the module it pulls in runs in the same content-script isolated world with the content-script `chrome.*` surface intact. List that module **and its whole transitive import graph** under `web_accessible_resources` (gated to the target origins) or the fetch is blocked — and have a test walk the graph from the entry module so a newly-added import can't silently fall out of the list.
61	- To put a menu on the **toolbar icon itself**, create it with `chrome.contextMenus.create({ contexts: ['action'], … })` — the `contextMenus` permission carries **no** install-time warning (unlike a broad host permission). Recreate the items with `contextMenus.removeAll()` first on install/startup so they self-heal instead of throwing on duplicate ids when the service worker re-runs its top level.
62	########## node/RULES.md
63	# Node.js
64	
65	Portable, project-agnostic practices for working in Node.js / npm codebases — package management, scripts, module resolution, runtime gotchas — true for any Node project read cold.
66	
67	## Module resolution
68	
69	- **A *named* import from a package's CommonJS entry can silently yield `undefined`.** Node recovers named bindings from a CJS module by static analysis, and that analysis fails on plenty of real entry points (a re-export built at runtime, a conditional assignment) — with no error: the import resolves, the binding is `undefined`, and the failure surfaces later as "x is not a function". When a package ships both entries, import the **ESM** one explicitly (`…/package/index.mjs`, or the `import` condition of its `exports`) for named bindings; when it doesn't, `import pkg from '…'` and destructure off the default. Resolve the package's own directory (`$(npm root -g)/<pkg>` for a global install) rather than hardcoding an absolute path into a version-pinned layout, which moves under you on the next image or upgrade.
70	- **Modern Node (22.7+) detects ES-module syntax in a `.js` file on its own** — no `"type": "module"`, no flag, no warning. A directory of ES modules therefore needs **no `package.json` of its own** just to be loadable; adding one to declare module-ness is cargo cult, and one already present for that reason is vestigial. (Prefer `.js` consistently within a tree over mixing in `.mjs` for the same purpose; the extension is then a style choice, not a signal.)
71	
72	## jsdom diverges from a real browser in ways a green test can hide
73	
74	Two that recur:
75	
76	- **`body.innerText` is null in jsdom.** Code reading `el.innerText || el.textContent` therefore falls through to `textContent` under test, which *includes* the `<script>` / `<style>` text, `<select>` / `<option>` text, and CSS-hidden text a real browser's `innerText` omits. Treat body-text results as jsdom-optimistic; never add a test that only passes because of it.
77	- **`runScripts: "outside-only"` (the default) parses `<noscript>` into live DOM — the opposite of a real browser.** A `textContent` read looks clean under test but splices the `<noscript>` markup into the value in Chrome, which keeps `<noscript>` as raw text. Parse a script-free fragment with `runScripts: "dangerously"` to reproduce the browser.

107	
108	# Testing practices
109	
110	Portable practices for writing tests you can actually trust — proving a test fails before relying on it, snapshot/golden discipline, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, and how to gate a fuzzy quality metric. These are project-agnostic; a consuming repo's own test *mechanics* (runner, layout, which suites exist) stay in its own docs. (General software-engineering practices live in [the engineering-practices skill](../engineering-practices/SKILL.md); CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md).)
111	
112	- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it.
113	- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. (A hostname-apex helper passed its tests but mis-stripped `tel-aviv.gov.il` → `gov.il`; the gap only surfaced when the function was run over the actual list of existing URLs.) Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once.
114	- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
115	- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
116	- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
117	- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (A UI-snapshot coverage gate parked behavioral leaves `9.1`–`9.3`/`3.4` and an unreachable `8.6` on cases that render none of them — issue #429.)
118	- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
119	- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
120	- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
121	- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
122	- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (The SPA-render fallback's CI test renders a `data:` URL whose script fills an empty root, not a real SPA — #310.)
123	- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
124	- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
125	- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
126	- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
127	- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
128	- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
129	- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

135	
136	# Engineering practices
137	
138	General software-engineering practices, independent of any one project. (These are portable, shared rules; project-specific rules — architecture, test mechanics — live in the consuming repo's own docs. The portable git/GitHub-operational practices — branch/commit history, merging, automated-job branches — live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md); the mechanics of searching and rewriting text across files — grep/sed sweeps, renames, broken references — live in [the repo-text-sweeps skill](../repo-text-sweeps/SKILL.md); and the practices for writing trustworthy tests — see-it-fail, snapshot/golden discipline, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, coverage gating — live in [the writing-tests skill](../writing-tests/SKILL.md); and how to investigate a bug and pin down its root cause — version-gap triage, re-deriving after a failed fix, probing for a real datapoint — lives in [the bug-investigation skill](../bug-investigation/SKILL.md).)
139	
140	- Name by scope/responsibility, not technology or mechanism.
141	- Keep a single source of truth for derived or duplicated data — generate the rest from it instead of hand-editing, and have a test fail if it drifts. Split a fact across more than one place only when a technological constraint forbids a single home, and then have the drift-guard test state, in its own text, the two-or-more places it watches and why the split is forced — so an invisible coupling becomes a self-documenting, reviewed one, and the next reader knows the duplication is deliberate and where its other half lives. When the duplicate mirrors executable logic you can't generate from (e.g. a static list shadowing a set of predicate/matcher functions), drift-guard it by *executing the real logic* against the list in both directions — every entry accepted by some predicate, and every predicate satisfied by some entry — rather than parsing the logic out. When a value must be copied into files that can't share an import (a label spanning a YAML workflow guard and a JS module; a repo slug in prod code and its test), declare it as a `sharedConstants` entry in `.claudinite-checks.json` — its `value`, the expected per-file `counts`, and a `what` naming the places and why — and the basics pack's `shared-constants` check enforces the counts, failing when a rename leaves some copies behind. It counts the *flat* literal (comments included), so keep a guarded value on one line wherever it appears — an occurrence wrapped across a line break is invisible to the check and to a `grep`/`sed` rename alike. For a value that must stay in sync but *changes over time* (a version string bumped each release), set `regex: true` and give a pattern instead of a literal — the check then requires every match to be identical across the declared files, so the guard never needs re-pinning on a bump.
142	- Honor separation of concerns in what you write — code comments and Markdown instructions alike: when file A uses or references file B (a module A imports, or a doc/procedure set A points to), A may state *what* it needs from B or *that* it delegates to B, but never restate *how* B does its job or re-spell the procedures B owns. B's mechanism lives in one place — with B. Copying it into A leaks B's internals across the boundary and springs the same drift trap as any duplicated source of truth: change B and A's paraphrase silently goes stale, with nothing to catch it. Point to B instead of paraphrasing it.
143	- One commit per concern: two changes that could each stand alone — separately revertible, cherry-pickable, bisectable — don't share a commit, and a message that numbers unrelated items is describing the split it should have been. More commits is not the goal: once a commit is in, later work is a *new* commit, never a rewrite of the one that landed.
144	- Name any file a test autogenerates with `GENERATED` in its filename (e.g. `foo.GENERATED.md`, `foo.baseline.GENERATED.json`) so it's unmistakable at a glance. Don't hand-edit a GENERATED file, and never resolve its merge conflict by hand: take either side to clear the markers, re-run the generator against the merged inputs, and commit its output. Hand-editing desyncs it from its source — and when the other branch changed the generator's logic, only a re-run produces correct values. Automate the "take either side" step itself where you can: assign the file a `merge=ours` `.gitattributes` entry (plus a one-time `git config merge.ours.driver true` per clone) so a conflicting merge on it resolves automatically instead of needing the markers cleared by hand first; `git config rerere.enabled true` similarly replays a manual conflict resolution automatically the next time the same conflict recurs.
145	- Verify how a platform or runtime actually behaves against authoritative docs or a real run — not against a comment or a prior commit's claim.
146	- Prove a *behaviour-preserving* optimisation actually preserves behaviour before trusting it — "it should be equivalent" is not evidence. Fingerprint the full outputs (hash them) and exercise the old and new paths across *every* branch (fuzz the inputs that select each), accepting the change only on a bit-identical match. And it is legitimate to leave a hot path un-optimised when the correctness risk of rewriting it outweighs the speed-up — record that as a deliberate call, not an oversight.
147	- Earn each dependency: prefer a built-in (or a few lines) for a narrow job, and drop one when the assumption that justified it lapses.

86:## An automated job needs a unique branch per run
88:An automated or scheduled job that derives its branch name from a non-unique key (e.g. the date) collides with itself on a repeat run for that key — `git checkout -b` fails when the branch already exists, and a push to the diverged remote branch is rejected non-fast-forward (so the run can't even open its PR). 106:A `push` or `workflow_dispatch` run isn't attached to a PR, so the PR-scoped check-run query above doesn't apply to it. Confirm such a run through the GitHub API/MCP tools: `get_job_logs(run_id, failed_only: true)` — "0 failed jobs" means green — or, for a release build, `get_release_by_tag`. Don't `curl` the run's status instead: in a sandboxed session `api.github.com` is proxy-blocked and returns an error body that never matches a success pattern, so a `curl`/`Monitor` poll silently reports "still running" until it times out.
